MIND.01.note: Article explains the effect and cites the source study; deeper is the original Norton/Mochon/Ariely paper. No video cleared the bar, so Watch stays on search.

deeper.title: The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love (Norton, Mochon & Ariely, 2012)
deeper.source: Norton, Mochon and Ariely — Harvard Business School

exercise.prompt: Compare how much you value two similar objects or outputs when you assembled one yourself, then identify effort, ownership and quality as competing explanations.

MIND.02.note: Jarrett is the definitive 'the pop story is overhyped' piece; deeper is the Kilner and Lemon review that the critique rests on. Video stays on search to avoid overclaiming.

article.title: Mirror Neurons: The Most Hyped Concept in Neuroscience?

deeper.title: What We Know Currently about Mirror Neurons
deeper.source: Kilner and Lemon — Current Biology / PubMed Central

exercise.prompt: Separate what mirror-neuron experiments directly measure from claims about imitation, empathy, language and autism, then label each claim as evidence, inference or speculation.

MIND.03.note: Schwartz's TED talk is the claim; Collins and the Scheibehenne meta-analysis provide the replication reality. Pairing them is the honest version of this topic.

deeper.title: Can There Ever Be Too Many Options? A Meta-Analytic Review of Choice Overload
deeper.source: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder and Todd — Journal of Consumer Research

exercise.prompt: Design a choice experiment that varies number of options while holding quality, familiarity and decision stakes constant, then define what would count as overload.

MIND.04.note: The hook frames synchronicity as contested and pattern hunger. The curated resource therefore explains patternicity rather than endorsing a supernatural interpretation.

article.title: Patternicity: Finding Meaningful Patterns in Meaningless Noise

exercise.prompt: Keep a one-week log of striking coincidences and also record the ordinary non-matches that could have become coincidences, then compare remembered hits with the full opportunity set.

MIND.05.note: Neuroplasticity is heavily hyped; Britannica supplies a sober overview that avoids the self-help claim that any habit can freely rewire any brain function.

exercise.prompt: Classify examples of plasticity as developmental, learning-related, compensatory or injury-related and identify biological constraints on each.

MIND.06.note: Britannica provides the concept; the deeper resource is Festinger and Carlsmith's founding forced-compliance experiment.

deeper.title: Cognitive Consequences of Forced Compliance
deeper.source: Festinger and Carlsmith — Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology / MIT

exercise.prompt: Map one inconsistency among belief, action and self-image, then list several possible dissonance-reduction strategies and the evidence each would leave behind.

MIND.07.note: The catalogue emphasizes the statistical critique, so the resource explains how random data, measurement boundaries and regression effects can reproduce the familiar graph.

article.title: The Dunning-Kruger Effect Is Probably Not Real
article.source: Jonathan Jarry — McGill Office for Science and Society

exercise.prompt: Generate random true scores and noisy self-assessments, group people by observed performance and graph average error to see how statistical artefacts can resemble the published effect.

MIND.08.note: Csikszentmihalyi's own TED talk supplies the primary popular account; BrainFacts provides a neuroscience-oriented secondary view without turning flow into a productivity guarantee.

article.title: Turning on Flow Means Turning Off Parts of the Brain

exercise.prompt: Choose one activity and vary challenge, skill, goals and feedback over several sessions, recording boredom, anxiety, absorption and performance rather than assuming flow occurred.

MIND.09.note: TED-Ed provides the accessible mechanism, NIH gives the overview, and the Rasch and Born review is the deeper open-access source on sleep-dependent memory consolidation.

video.title: The Benefits of a Good Night's Sleep

article.title: Sleep On It: How Snoozing Strengthens Memories

deeper.title: About Sleep's Role in Memory
deeper.source: Rasch and Born — Physiological Reviews / PubMed Central

exercise.prompt: Learn two matched sets of material before sleep and before an equally long waking interval, test delayed recall and identify the controls needed before attributing differences to consolidation.

MIND.10.note: Anil Seth supplies the accessible on-ramp to predictive perception; Andy Clark's review is the field-defining deeper treatment of prediction, action and error correction.

video.title: Your Brain Hallucinates Your Conscious Reality

article.title: The Hard Problem of Consciousness Is a Distraction from the Real One

deeper.title: Whatever Next? Predictive Brains, Situated Agents, and the Future of Cognitive Science
deeper.source: Andy Clark — Behavioral and Brain Sciences / UCL

exercise.prompt: Use one ambiguous image or sound to describe prior expectation, sensory evidence, prediction error and how changing context alters the final percept.

MIND.11.note: Nielsen's essay is the strongest single practical treatment of spaced repetition as a system for building long-term understanding rather than merely memorizing isolated trivia.

exercise.prompt: Create ten atomic retrieval cards from one difficult concept, schedule them over two weeks and revise cards that produce guessing, ambiguity or rote wording without understanding.

MIND.12.note: The resource debunks the fabricated '38 silent witnesses' version of Kitty Genovese and summarizes modern evidence showing that help is common and can increase with more bystanders.

article.title: The Bystander Effect Started from a Lie
article.source: Jonathan Jarry — McGill Office for Science and Society

exercise.prompt: Break an emergency response into noticing, interpreting, taking responsibility, knowing what to do and acting, then design instructions that reduce ambiguity at each stage.
